messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Martin Weber, a 55-year-old counselor who had spent most of his adult life helping other people steady themselves in crisis, came to treatment after months of feeling that his own mind and body had become unreliable. The event he returned to, reluctantly and only in fragments, was a fire set intentionally in the counseling center where he worked. Late one evening, after a tense confrontation elsewhere in the building, he had smelled smoke before he understood what was happening. By the time he opened his office door, there was a harsh burnt odor in the hallway, alarms blaring, and somewhere down the corridor the crash of objects being hurled as people tried to force open a jammed exit and clear a path. He remembered the confusion less as a sequence than as sensations: the scorched smell, the impact sounds, the certainty that danger had already entered the building before anyone could get ahead of it.

In the weeks that followed, those sensory details began intruding into ordinary life. At work, if a patient knocked a water bottle off a table or a file was tossed into a bin, Martin felt his whole attention snap toward the sound of an object being thrown. If he passed a break room where toast had burned or caught even a faint smoke smell outside the building, he would feel the emotional force of that night hit him all at once, often without any picture in his mind. Sometimes, when he tried to explain this, he said it was as though the feeling arrived first—raw fear, urgency, a sense that something terrible was underway—and only later, if at all, did any recognizable memory follow. At other moments, simply thinking about the fire brought back the smell itself so vividly that he found himself checking the room, convinced for a second that something nearby was burning.

He had come to believe that his body was now working against him. What frightened him most was not only the memory of the fire, but the way his chest tightened, his stomach dropped, and his attention narrowed whenever he encountered those cues, even in settings that were objectively safe. To Martin, these reactions meant his system still “thought” he was in danger; he said bitterly that his body kept reacting as if the event were present tense. From there it made sense to him that he had to stay especially careful because you never knew what might happen next. The more he watched himself for signs of losing control, the stranger the memory became. He sometimes described it as if it belonged to someone else, as though he were reporting on a case rather than recalling his own experience, yet the emotional intensity remained immediate and unmuted.

Because he was certain that deliberately thinking about the fire would overwhelm him, Martin began organizing his days around not letting his mind go there. He cut short conversations with friends who asked how he was doing and gradually stopped seeing them at all, partly because he did not want to be asked direct questions and partly because social gatherings felt full of unpredictable noises and smells. In session rooms at the counseling center, he positioned himself near the door and kept a private watch on his thoughts, scanning for any sign that he might be “going crazy” if the memory surfaced. That constant monitoring did not calm him. It made him more aware of the moments when the burnt smell seemed to come back from nowhere or when a wave of fear surged up without an image, which only confirmed his sense that the event was lodged somewhere beyond his control. The more he tried not to think about it, the more the memory returned in these disjointed sensory and emotional forms.

Over months, the loop tightened. A smell of smoke in the parking lot could pull up the memory’s odor with startling force, and once that happened he became even more convinced that ordinary cues were dangerous and that his body could not be trusted. A clatter in the office—someone angrily throwing a stack of folders into a cabinet—could leave him preoccupied for the rest of the day, avoiding colleagues and redoubling his efforts to keep the event out of mind. His work began to suffer in the quiet ways that embarrassed him most: he was less present with clients, more distracted by scanning his own internal state, and increasingly isolated in a profession built on human contact.

What finally brought Martin in was a moment of humiliation after he smelled something burnt in the staff kitchen and had to leave abruptly before meeting with a client. He was shaken less by the interruption than by what it seemed to prove to him—that even now, a smell or a sound could reach inside him and pull him back into an experience that did not feel fully his and yet still overwhelmed him. He said he wanted help because he was tired of living as if catastrophe were always about to break through the next ordinary moment. What he feared most was that if he ever let himself face the event directly, he would not be able to handle what came up. What he hoped, quietly, was to stop feeling ambushed by his own mind.
